title: Physical Applications
lead: Cutting an object into small pieces turns a physical quantity into a definite integral: the mass of a rod or a disk from its density function, the work done by a variable force such as a spring’s or in pumping a liquid out of a tank, and the hydrostatic force of a liquid on a submerged plate, up to the face of the Hoover Dam.
objectives: Determine the mass of a one-dimensional object from its linear density function.
Determine the mass of a two-dimensional circular object from its radial density function.
Calculate the work done by a variable force acting along a line.
Calculate the work done in pumping a liquid from one height to another.
Find the hydrostatic force against a submerged vertical plate.
summary_html:
• Several physical applications of the definite integral are common in engineering and physics.
  • Definite integrals can be used to determine the mass of an object if its density function is known.
  • Work can also be calculated from integrating a force function, or when counteracting the force of gravity, as in a pumping problem.
  • Definite integrals can also be used to calculate the force exerted on an object submerged in a liquid.

State your answers with three significant figures. (Note: $G=6.67\;\times \;{10}^{-11}\;{\text{N m}}^{2}/{\text{kg}}^{2}$ and $M=6\;\times \;{10}^{24}\;\text{kg}.)$

[T] A rectangular dam is $40$ ft high and $60$ ft wide. Assume the weight density of water is 62.5 lbs/ft3. Compute the total force $F$ on the dam when

  1. the surface of the water is at the top of the dam and
  2. the surface of the water is halfway down the dam.
[T] Find the work required to pump all the water out of the cylinder in the preceding exercise if the cylinder is only half full.
A cylinder of depth $H$ and cross-sectional area $A$ stands full of water at density $\rho.$ Compute the work to pump all the water to the top.
A cone-shaped tank has a cross-sectional area that increases with its depth: $A=(\pi r^{2}h^{2})/H^{3}.$ Show that the work to empty it is half the work for a cylinder with the same height and base.

answer.solution: Measure $x$ down from the top, so a layer at depth $x$ is lifted $x$ to the top and, with weight density $\rho,$ weighs $\rho A(x)\,\Delta x.$ For the cone, with radius $r$ at the bottom $x=H,$ the layer at depth $x$ has area $A(x)=\pi r^{2}x^{2}/H^{2}$. Then $W_{\text{cone}}=\int_{0}^{H}\rho\frac{\pi r^{2}x^{2}}{H^{2}}x\,dx=\frac{\rho\pi r^{2}}{H^{2}}\cdot\frac{H^{4}}{4}=\frac{\rho\pi r^{2}H^{2}}{4}.$ For the cylinder of the same height and base, every layer has area $\pi r^{2},$ so $W_{\text{cyl}}=\int_{0}^{H}\rho\pi r^{2}x\,dx=\frac{\rho\pi r^{2}H^{2}}{2}.$ The cone’s work is half the cylinder’s.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

The amount of work to pump the water out of a half-full cylinder is half the amount of work to pump the water out of the full cylinder.

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If the force is constant, the amount of work to move an object from $x=a$ to $x=b$ is $F(b-a).$

answer.solution: True. A constant force $F$ is the constant function $F(x)=F,$ so $W=\int_{a}^{b}F\,dx=F(b-a).$
